# PhysicsWallah’s losses widen in FY24 as rising expenses overshadow 2.6X revenue growth

## The Noida-based company also revised its FY 2022-23 figures, now reporting a loss of Rs 84.1 crore, in contrast to the Rs 8.9 crore profit previously stated in its earlier consolidated financial statements.

![Photo of Ishan Patra](https://images.yourstory.com/cs/users/d99b1110-1169-11ed-9e63-f54395117598/google/profile_image_1774860800170.jpg?format=auto&w=96&q=75)[Ishan Patra](/author/ishan-patra)[927 Stories](/author/ishan-patra)

![PhysicsWallah’s losses widen in FY24 as rising expenses overshadow 2.6X revenue growth](https://images.yourstory.com/cs/2/d99b1110116911ed9e63f54395117598/USETHIS--NewPPTTemplates1-1726753378569.png?mode=fit&crop=faces&ar=16%3A9&format=auto&w=1920&q=75)

Thursday November 07, 2024, 4 min Read

[![Google Preferred](https://images.yourstory.com/assets/images/google_preferred.webp?format=auto&w=384&q=75)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=yourstory.com)

Edtech unicorn [PhysicsWallah](https://yourstory.com/tag/physicswallah) (PW) saw its losses widen significantly in FY 2023-24, fueled by a sharp rise in employee benefit costs and other expenditures, casting a shadow over a 2.6-fold increase in operating revenue.

The Noida-based company also revised its FY 2022-23 figures, now reporting a loss of Rs 84.1 crore, in contrast to the Rs 8.9 crore profit previously stated in its earlier consolidated financial statements.

The heavy losses come on the back of the edtech company’s rapid expansion over the past couple of years. PW, which initially focused on the test-prep segment, has rapidly diversified its educational offerings over the past few years to encompass everything—from [school](https://yourstory.com/2024/03/physicswallah-schools-wants-catch-em-young-alakh-pandey) education to [skills](https://yourstory.com/2023/08/physicswallah-betting-big-skilling-alakh-pandey-simplilearn-upgrad-eruditus) training—casting its learning net over a wide base of learners.

PW’s rapid expansion comes amid a turbulent period for BYJU’S, once the leading [edtech](https://yourstory.com/tag/edtech) platform and the poster child of the Indian startup ecosystem.

The [Alakh Pandey](https://yourstory.com/tag/alakh-pandey)-led firm reported a consolidated loss of Rs 1,131.3 crore in FY24, up 13.5X from Rs 84.1 crore recorded in the earlier fiscal period.

The reported losses were impacted by non-cash adjustments, such as Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS) amounting to Rs 756 crore, according to the company. This CCPS expense is recorded in relation to the buyback clause provided in the issued CCPS, based on the conversion of accounting standards from IGAAP to INDAS, it added.

After excluding the non-cash adjustment, the company’s actual cash losses come to approximately Rs 375 crore, up 4.4X.

The company had remained the only profitable edtech firm until FY22, while steadily growing its top line.

Its operating revenue surged 160.7%, touching Rs 1,940.4 crore in FY24 compared to Rs 744.3 crore in FY23, as per its recent consolidated financial statements.

The startup’s total income reached Rs 2,015.1 crore, up 160.8% increase year-on-year (YoY).

For context, BYJU’S surpassed the Rs 2,000 crore revenue mark in FY20 and Eruditus in FY23, while PW achieved this milestone in its fourth year of operations. BYJU’S was incorporated in 2011, Eruditus in 2010, and PW in 2020.

Meanwhile, the company’s expenses surged by 280.4% to Rs 3,279.1 crore in FY24 compared with Rs 862 crore in FY23.

The sharp rise in expenses was driven by employee benefits, the firm’s second-largest cost centre, which jumped to Rs 1,159 crore—a 180.9% YoY.

Its other expenses surged by 442.4% YoY to Rs 1,660 crore, including a significant increase in miscellaneous expenses, which rose by 755.9% to Rs 1,452.7 crore.

Interestingly, PW also reduced its advertising and promotional expenses by 39.9%, although these still accounted for the company’s second-largest expense, totalling Rs 37.3 crore in FY24 compared with Rs 62.1 crore in FY23.

PW has experienced impressive growth, however, sustainable growth and profitability are essential, and it must navigate its own challenges as it expands.

Earlier this year, PW Co-founder Prateek Maheshwari told *YourStory* that FY24 was the year of “growth,” while FY25 is the year of “sustainable growth,” as PW aims to return to a profitable path.

“We have bounced back this year, with the first two quarters being EBITDA profitable for the first time in our company’s history,” he added. EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, is a measure of core operational efficiency.

While the profitability metric for FY25 cannot be determined due to the transition from I-GAAP to Ind-AS, this fiscal year is expected to be the highest in absolute EBITDA profitability since inception, according to Maheshwari.

I-GAAP (Indian Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) refers to the traditional accounting standards used in the country, while Ind-AS (Indian Accounting Standards) is a set of accounting standards aligned with IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) for greater transparency and consistency.

In September, PW raised [$210 million](https://yourstory.com/2024/09/edtech-physicswallah-funding-alakh-pandey-hornbill-lightspeed-westbridge-gsv) in a Series B funding round led by investment firm Hornbill Capital, with a sizable participation from venture capital firm Lightspeed Venture Partners. This was a significant milestone given the scarcity of substantial deals in India’s edtech sector lately.

With the latest funding round, PW’s post-money valuation has [soared](https://yourstory.com/2022/06/the-turning-point-edtech-startup-physicswallah-unicorn) to $2.8 billion, making it the third-most valued edtech firm, trailing only Unacademy ($3.4 billion) and Eruditus ($3.2 billion), based on their last valuations.

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Controladora Vuela Compañía de Aviación, S.A.B. de C.V. (NYSE: VLRS and BMV: VOLAR) (“Volaris” or “the Company”), the ultra-low-cost carrier (ULCC) serving Mexico, the United States, Central and South America, today reports its unaudited financial results for the third quarter 20261.

Enrique Beltranena, President & Chief Executive Officer, said: “Our strong commercial performance in the third quarter marked a historic milestone for Volaris: we achieved double-digit TRASM for the first time in our history, with quarterly operating revenues crossing the US$1 billion mark, driven by both ancillary growth and fare strength. We entered the summer peak with a clear plan—and delivered. Strong demand absorbed our additional capacity, while our expanding transborder network, disciplined capacity allocation, and improving aircraft productivity reinforced our competitive position.

We delivered positive EBIT, an outcome not anticipated in our original outlook, and reduced our net loss by nearly 80% sequentially. Despite higher-than-anticipated fuel costs, we preserved US$823 million in liquidity, broadly unchanged quarter-over-quarter. Together, these achievements validate our strategy and reinforce the strength and resilience of our ultra-low-cost model, and our ability to turn disciplined execution into tangible results.”

Third Quarter 2026   
(All figures are reported in U.S. dollars and compared to 3Q 2025, unless otherwise noted)

Total operating revenues for the quarter amounted to $1,038 million, up by 32.4%.

Total capacity, in terms of available seat miles (ASMs ), was 10.1 billion, representing an 11.1% increase.

Booked passengers totaled 9.0 million, a 14.3% increase. Mexican domestic booked passengers increased 13.7%, while international booked passengers increased 16.0%.

TRASM increased 19.2% to 10.31 cents, primarily driven by a 25.5% increase in average base fare, which  
reached $55 during the quarter. TRASM was further supported by an 8.4% increase in total ancillary revenue per passenger, which stood at $61.

Total operating revenue per passenger totaled $116, increasing 15.8%. During the quarter, ancillary revenues represented 52.8% of total operating revenues.

The load factor for the quarter reached 85.7%, representing a 1.3 percentage point increase.

Total operating expenses were $1,004 million, compared with $716 million in the previous year.

CASM totaled 9.97 cents, up 26.2%.

The average economic fuel cost increased 57.4%, reaching $4.10 per gallon.

CASM ex fuel stood at 6.23 cents, up 13.7% year-over-year, but below guidance, supported by improved fixed-cost absorption from higher-than-planned capacity and continued cost efficiencies.

Comprehensive financing result represented an expense of $75 million, compared to a $59 million expense in the same period of 2025.

Income tax benefit was $15 million, compared with a $3 million expense recorded in the third quarter of 2025. The Company expects the effective tax rate to be approximately in line with the statutory rate by the end of the fiscal year.

Net loss in the quarter was $26 million, with loss per ADS of 23 cents.

EBITDAR for the quarter reached $263 million, representing a 0.4% decrease. EBITDAR margin stood at 25.3%, down 8.3 percentage points.

Balance Sheet, Liquidity, and Capital Allocation

As of September 30, 2026, cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $823 million, representing 23.2% of the last twelve months' total operating revenue.

Net cash flow provided by operating and investing activities was $234 million and $36 million, respectively. Net cash flow used in financing activities was $271 million.

The financial debt amounted to $598 million, reflecting a decrease of 14.9% compared to the end of 2025, while total lease liabilities increased slightly by 1.4% to $3,196 million.

Net debt-to-LTM EBITDAR 4 ratio stood at 3.3x, unchanged from the previous quarter, and compared to 3.1x at the end of 2025.

The average exchange rate for the quarter was Ps.17.25 per U.S. dollar, reflecting a 7.5% appreciation of the Mexican peso. At the end of September, the exchange rate stood at Ps.17.84 per U.S. dollar, compared to Ps. 18.38 per U.S. dollar in the previous year, reflecting a 2.9% appreciation of the Mexican peso.

We also declared a $0.25 per share cash dividend, $0.05 more than those declared in 2025, reinforcing our commitment to shareholder value.

Five Star Bank’s success reflects the strength of our team and the value of authentic, relationship-based service. Our technology, operating discipline, conservative underwriting, strong credit quality, and prudent portfolio management position us to create lasting value for customers, employees, communities, and shareholders. Three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to three months ended June 30, 2026

The Company’s net income was $21.9 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to $19.4 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026. Net interest income increased by $4.8 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended June 30, 2026, primarily reflecting growth in higher-yielding loans and an increase in the yield on interest-earning assets, partially offset by higher deposit funding costs. The provision for credit losses increased by $0.3 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended June 30, 2026, reflecting loan growth and changes resulting from the annual Current Expected Credit Loss (“CECL”) model refresh. Non-interest income decreased by $0.2 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended June 30, 2026, primarily due to an overall decline in earnings related to investments in venture-backed funds and lower loan referral income, partially offset by a special FHLB stock dividend. Non-interest expense increased by $1.0 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended June 30, 2026, primarily due to higher salaries and employee benefits from increased headcount and increased recruiter fees, partially offset by decreases in employee-related expenses, advertising and promotional expenses, and operational losses.

Three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to three months ended September 30, 2025

The Company’s net income was $21.9 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to $16.3 million for the three months ended September 30, 2025. Net interest income increased by $11.6 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended September 30, 2025, primarily reflecting balance sheet growth and lower deposit funding costs following three Federal Reserve rate cuts that began in September 2025, partially offset by lower yields on interest-earning assets. The provision for credit losses remained constant, reflecting loan growth and changes resulting from the annual CECL model refresh, offset by a decrease in the provision for unfunded commitments. Non-interest income decreased by $0.3 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended September 30, 2025, primarily reflecting lower fees from swap referrals and an overall decline in earnings related to investments in venture-backed funds. Non-interest expense increased by $4.0 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026, as compared to the three months ended September 30, 2025, driven primarily by higher salaries and employee benefits from increased headcount, along with growth in other operating expenses reflecting continued organizational expansion.

Net interest income during the three months ended September 30, 2026 increased by $4.8 million, or 10.51%, to $50.9 million, as compared to $46.1 million during the three months ended June 30, 2026. Net interest margin totaled 3.69% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, an increase of six basis points compared to the prior quarter, primarily reflecting growth in higher-yielding loans and an increase in the yield on interest-earning assets, partially offset by higher deposit funding costs. The $4.8 million increase in net interest income is primarily attributable to a $376.7 million, or 7.39%, increase in average interest-earning assets. The average balance of loans increased $284.3 million, or 6.57%, and the average balance of interest-earning deposits in banks increased $95.7 million, or 14.14%. The average yield on interest-earning assets increased five basis points to 5.74%, including a six-basis-point increase in the average loan yield to 6.14%. The increase in interest income was partially offset by a $2.0 million increase in interest expense. The average balance of deposits increased $257.9 million, or 5.55%, combined with a three-basis-point increase in the average cost of deposits. The average balance of non-interest bearing deposits increased $48.1 million, or 4.13%, helping to partially offset the rise in deposit funding costs.

As compared to the three months ended September 30, 2025, net interest income during the three months ended September 30, 2026 increased by $11.6 million, or 29.42%, to $50.9 million from $39.3 million. Net interest margin totaled 3.69% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, an increase of 13 basis points compared to the same quarter of the prior year. The increase primarily reflected balance sheet growth and lower deposit funding costs following three Federal Reserve rate cuts that began in September 2025, partially offset by lower yields on interest-earning assets. The increase in net interest income is primarily attributable to a $14.3 million increase in interest income, mainly due to a $780.8 million, or 20.38%, increase in the average balance of loans and a $321.4 million, or 71.17%, increase in the average balance of interest-earning deposits in banks. The benefit from higher average earning assets was partially offset by a 13-basis-point decrease in the yield on interest-earning assets to 5.74%. The average loan yield remained stable at 6.14%, as the effect of lower rates on repricing loans was offset by loan growth and changes in portfolio mix. This increase in interest income was partially offset by a $2.8 million increase in interest expense, stemming from a $946.6 million, or 23.89%, increase in the average balance of deposits during the three months ended September 30, 2026, moderated by a 25-basis-point decrease in the average cost of deposits compared to the same quarter of the prior year, reflecting deposit repricing following the three Federal Reserve rate cuts that began in September 2025 and an improved funding mix. Further supporting the decreasing average cost of deposits, the average balance of non-interest-bearing deposits increased by $195.5 million, or 19.23%, and brokered deposits decreased from $216.4 million to zero compared to the same period of the prior year.

MINNEAPOLIS, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Alerus Financial Corporation (Nasdaq: ALRS), or the Company, reported net income of $19.2 million for the third quarter of 2026, or $0.76 per diluted common share, compared to net income of $20.9 million, or $0.81 per diluted common share, for the second quarter of 2026, and net income of $16.9 million, or $0.65 per diluted common share, for the third quarter of 2025.

CEO Comments

President and Chief Executive Officer Katie O'Neill Lorenson said, "Our third quarter results demonstrate the continued momentum of the Alerus franchise, with strong revenue growth across our diversified business model and strategic organic growth in our banking franchise. Net interest income increased 8.3% from the prior year, while noninterest income grew 16.7%, reflecting the complementary strength of our banking, retirement and benefit services, and wealth advisory businesses.

That growth was driven by the continued transformation of our banking franchise toward commercial and business banking. Commercial and business lending grew 36.5% from a year ago and now represents 37.1% of our loan portfolio, up from 27.7% a year ago. In the third quarter, total loans increased $150.5 million, or 3.7%, and deposits increased $111.2 million, or 2.7%, with noninterest income representing 42.4% of total revenue.

We also maintained favorable credit quality, with nonperforming assets and criticized loans continuing to improve and net recoveries during the quarter. Our strong capital position and 10.9% year-over-year growth in tangible book value per share give us the capacity to keep investing in organic growth while returning capital to shareholders, with $37.2 million returned through dividends and share repurchases in the first nine months of the year.

Most importantly, I want to thank our team members. Their talent, collaboration, and focus on helping clients achieve their goals turn our strategy into results, and we are confident in our continued ability to create sustainable value for clients, communities, team members, and shareholders."

Third Quarter Highlights

■
Earnings per diluted common share of $0.76.

■
Return on average total assets of 1.45%.

■
Return on average tangible common equity(1) of 17.35%.

■
Noninterest income was $34.4 million in the third quarter of 2026, an increase of 4.3% from the second quarter of 2026. Noninterest income represented 42.4% of total revenue in the third quarter of 2026.

■
Net interest margin (on a tax-equivalent basis)(1) was 3.84% and net interest income was $46.7 million in the third quarter of 2026.

■
Total loans were $4.2 billion as of September 30, 2026, an increase of $150.5 million, or 3.7%, from June 30, 2026.

■
Total deposits were $4.3 billion as of September 30, 2026, an increase of $111.2 million, or 2.7%, from June 30, 2026.

■
Nonperforming assets were $16.4 million as of September 30, 2026, a decrease of $0.7 million, or 4.3%, from $17.1 million as of June 30, 2026.

■
Net recoveries to average loans was 0.10%.

■
Repurchased $8.2 million of the Company's outstanding common stock at an average per share price of $32.75, reducing common shares outstanding by 250,000 shares at quarter-end.

■
In the first nine months of 2026, the Company returned $37.2 million to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases.

■
In the first nine months of 2026, adjusted pre-provision net revenue(1) was $78.7 million, an 18.9% increase over the same time period in the prior year.

■
Total assets under management/administration in the combined retirement and benefit and wealth segments were $50.1 billion, a 2.7% increase from September 30, 2025.

■
Tangible book value per common share(1) was $18.74 as of September 30, 2026, an increase of 10.9% from $16.90 as of September 30, 2025.

■

Results of Operations

Net Interest Income

Net interest income for the third quarter of 2026 was $46.7 million, a $1.0 million, or 2.1%, decrease from the second quarter of 2026. Interest income decreased $0.4 million, or 0.6%, primarily due to lower interest income on loans from a one-time $1.6 million interest income recovery on a nonaccrual loan resolution in the second quarter and less purchase accounting accretion, partially offset by higher loan and investment yields. Interest expense increased $0.6 million, or 2.4%, from the second quarter of 2026, as average rates paid on deposits and borrowings increased slightly, mainly driven by the recent increase by the Federal Reserve in the federal funds benchmark rate.

Net interest income increased $3.6 million, or 8.3%, from $43.1 million for the third quarter of 2025. Interest income decreased $0.5 million, or 0.6%, from the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by less purchase accounting accretion and lower average interest-bearing cash balances, partially offset by higher interest income on investment securities following the strategic balance sheet repositioning in the fourth quarter of 2025. Interest expense decreased $4.0 million, or 14.7%, from the third quarter of 2025, as average rates paid on deposits and borrowings declined primarily driven by Federal Reserve rate cuts in the second half of 2025.

Net interest margin (on a tax-equivalent basis)(1) was 3.84% for the third quarter of 2026, a 13 basis point decrease from 3.97% for the second quarter of 2026, and a 34 basis point increase from 3.50% for the third quarter of 2025. The quarter over quarter decrease was mainly attributable to a one-time $1.6 million interest income recovery on a nonaccrual loan resolution in the second quarter and less purchase accounting accretion, partially offset by higher loan and investment yields. The increase from the third quarter of 2025 was primarily driven by lower cost of funds and higher yields on investment securities, offset by less purchase accounting accretion.

Noninterest Income

Noninterest income for the third quarter of 2026 was $34.4 million, a $1.4 million, or 4.3%, increase from the second quarter of 2026. This increase was driven by increases in other noninterest income, retirement and benefit services revenue, wealth advisory services revenue, and mortgage banking revenue. Other noninterest income increased $0.5 million, or 15.1%, from the second quarter of 2026, primarily driven by a gain on the sale of a property in the Fargo, North Dakota market, partially offset by a loss on a property transferred to held for sale in the Rochester, Minnesota market. Retirement and benefit services revenue increased $0.3 million, or 1.8%, compared to the second quarter of 2026, primarily driven by an increase in recurring annual revenue. Wealth advisory services revenue increased $0.3 million, or 3.8%, from the second quarter of 2026, primarily driven by an increase in transaction-based fees and a slight increase in asset-based revenues. Mortgage banking revenue increased $0.1 million, or 4.2%, from the second quarter of 2026, primarily driven by higher mortgage originations and gain on sale margins.

Noninterest income for the third quarter of 2026 increased by $4.9 million, or 16.7%, from the third quarter of 2025. This increase was driven by increases in other noninterest income, retirement and benefit services revenue, wealth advisory services revenue, and service charges on deposit accounts. Other noninterest income increased $1.9 million, or 85.3%, compared to the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by a gain on the sale of a property in the Fargo, North Dakota market, partially offset by a loss on a property transferred to held for sale in the Rochester, Minnesota market. Retirement and benefit services revenue increased $1.2 million, or 7.1%, compared to the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by recurring annual income. Wealth advisory services revenue increased $1.4 million, or 22.0%, from the third quarter of 2025, driven by an increase in both asset-based fees and transaction-based fees. Wealth advisory services assets under administration/management increased $351.4 million, or 7.3% during the same period. Service charges on deposit accounts increased $0.5 million, or 73.7%, compared to the third quarter of 2025, primarily due to a reclassification of fees from other noninterest income to service charges on deposit accounts revenue in the first quarter of 2026.

Noninterest Expense

Noninterest expense for the third quarter of 2026 was $53.9 million, a $1.0 million, or 1.9%, increase from the second quarter of 2026. About Alerus Financial Corporation

Alerus Financial Corporation (Nasdaq: ALRS) is a commercial wealth advisory services bank and national retirement and benefit services provider with corporate offices in Grand Forks, North Dakota, and the Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota metropolitan area. Through its subsidiary, Alerus Financial, National Association (the “Bank”), Alerus provides diversified and comprehensive financial solutions to business and consumer clients, including banking, wealth advisory services, and retirement and benefit plans and services. Alerus provides clients with a primary point of contact to help fully understand their unique needs and delivery channel preferences. Clients are provided with competitive products, valuable insight, and sound advice supported by digital solutions designed to meet their needs.

Alerus operates 25 banking and commercial wealth offices, with locations in Grand Forks and Fargo, North Dakota; the Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota metropolitan area; Rochester, Minnesota; Southern Minnesota; Marshalltown, Iowa; Pewaukee, Wisconsin; and Tempe and Scottsdale, Arizona. The Alerus Retirement and Benefit business serves advisors, brokers, employers, and plan participants across the United States.

HOQUIAM, Wash., Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Timberland Bancorp, Inc. (NASDAQ: TSBK) (“Timberland” or “the Company”), the holding company for Timberland Bank (the “Bank”), today reported net income of $31.17 million for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2026, an increase of 7% from $29.16 million for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2025. Earnings per diluted common share (“EPS”) increased 8% to $3.96 for the 2026 fiscal year from $3.67 for the 2025 fiscal year.

Timberland also reported net income of $8.11 million, or $1.04 per diluted common share for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. This compares to net income of $7.72 million, or $0.98 per diluted common share for the preceding quarter, and $8.45 million, or $1.07 per diluted common share, for the comparable quarter one year ago. (Note: net income for the comparable quarter one year ago was increased by a $1.04 million bank owned life insurance benefit claim.)

“We closed out the fiscal year on a high note, delivering record annual earnings per share and a strong fourth quarter,” stated Dean Brydon, Chief Executive Officer. “Net income and earnings per share increased 5% and 6%, respectively, from the prior quarter, while net interest margin widened compared with both the prior quarter and year-ago quarter. While earnings were lower than the year-ago quarter, that period included a $1.04 million BOLI insurance claim, and excluding that benefit, results compared favorably. For the full fiscal year, we also improved our net interest margin and return on average assets while generating solid growth in net loans. We are proud of what our team accomplished this year in serving our customers, communities, and shareholders, and we look forward to building on that progress in the new year.”

“As a result of Timberland’s strong earnings and capital position, our Board of Directors announced a 3% increase to the quarterly cash dividend to shareholders of $0.31 per share, payable on November 27, 2026, to shareholders of record on November 12, 2026,” stated Jonathan Fischer, President and Chief Operating Officer. “Marking our 56th consecutive quarterly cash dividend, this payment reflects the Board’s continued confidence in Timberland’s long-term prospects.”

“Overall, fourth quarter earnings were strong and largely free of non-recurring items,” said Marci Basich, Chief Financial Officer. “Revenue generation was strong and net interest margin expanded 11 basis points from the prior quarter and 14 basis points from the year-ago quarter, reflecting our disciplined approach to pricing on both sides of the balance sheet. We also continued to build shareholder value during the quarter, growing tangible book value per share (non-GAAP) to $33.54, while repurchasing 40,395 shares of our common stock. These actions, combined with the dividend increase, reflect both the strength of our earnings and our confidence in the long-term value of the franchise.”

“Net loans grew 2% from the prior quarter, a testament to the strength of our lending teams and the continued demand we are seeing in our markets,” Brydon continued. “Credit quality held steady with modest improvements in non-performing asset levels, delinquency levels, and substandard loan levels. While net charge-offs increased, that was largely the result of charging off specific reserves we had already set up on several loans in prior periods. Our markets continue to offer solid growth opportunities and we remain confident in the quality of our loan portfolio and our disciplined approach to credit risk management.”

Operating Results

Operating revenue (net interest income before the provision for credit losses plus non-interest income) for the current quarter increased 5% to $22.79 million from $21.79 million for the preceding quarter and increased 1% from $22.49 million for the comparable quarter one year ago. The increase in operating revenue compared to the preceding quarter was primarily due to an increase in interest income on loans receivable, and to a lesser extent, an increase in non-interest income. These increases in operating revenue were partially offset by a decrease in interest income on interest-bearing deposits in banks, and to a lesser extent, an increase in interest expense. Operating revenue increased 6%, to $87.34 million for the 2026 fiscal year from $82.55 million for the 2025 fiscal year, primarily due to increases in interest income on loans receivable and interest income on interest-bearing deposits in banks, and a decrease in interest expense. These increases in operating revenue for the fiscal year were partially offset by decreases in interest income on investment securities and net BOLI earnings.

Net interest income increased $857,000 or 5%, to $19.66 million for the current quarter from $18.81 million for the preceding quarter and increased $1.27 million, or 7%, from $18.40 million for the comparable quarter one year ago. The increase in net interest income compared to the preceding quarter was primarily due to an $11.46 million increase in the average interest-earning assets, a nine-basis point increase in the weighted average yield on interest-bearing assets and, to a lesser extent, a one-basis point decrease in the weighted average cost of interest-bearing liabilities. Net interest income for the 2026 fiscal year increased $5.46 million, or 8%, to $75.66 million from $70.20 million for the 2025 fiscal year, primarily due to an $89.24 million increase in average interest-earning assets and a 17-basis point decrease in the weighted average cost of interest-bearing liabilities.

Timberland’s NIM for the current quarter increased to 3.96% from 3.85% for the preceding quarter and from 3.82% for the comparable quarter one year ago. The NIM for the current quarter was increased by approximately two basis points due to the collection of $94,000 in pre-payment penalties, non-accrual interest, and late fees, and the accretion of $8,000 of the fair value discount on acquired loans. The NIM for the preceding quarter was increased by approximately two basis points due to the collection of $82,000 in pre-payment penalties, non-accrual interest, and late fees, and the accretion of $8,000 of the fair value discount on acquired loans. The NIM for the comparable quarter one year ago was increased by approximately two basis points due to the collection of $102,000 in pre-payment penalties, non-accrual interest, and late fees, and the accretion of $11,000 of the fair value discount on acquired loans. Timberland’s NIM expanded to 3.87% for fiscal year 2026 from 3.76% for fiscal year 2025.

A $475,000 provision for credit losses on loans was recorded for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. The provision was primarily due to loan portfolio growth and changes in the composition of the loan portfolio. This compares to a $600,000 provision for credit losses on loans for the preceding quarter and a $213,000 provision for credit losses on loans for the comparable quarter one year ago.

Non-interest income increased $134,000, or 4%, to $3.12 million for the current quarter from $2.99 million for the preceding quarter and decreased $971,000, or 24%, from $4.09 million for the comparable quarter one year ago. The increase in non-interest income compared to the preceding quarter was primarily due to a $99,000 increase in BOLI net earnings and smaller increases in several other categories. Non-interest income for the 2026 fiscal year decreased by 5%, to $11.68 million from $12.35 million for the 2025 fiscal year. The decrease in non-interest income compared to the prior year periods was primarily the result of a $1.04 million BOLI death benefit claim recorded in the comparable quarter one year ago.

Total operating (non-interest) expenses for the current quarter increased $652,000, or 6%, to $12.29 million from $11.64 million for the preceding quarter and increased $331,000, or 3%, from $11.96 million for the comparable quarter one year ago. The increase in operating expenses compared to the preceding quarter was primarily due to increases in salary and employee benefits expense and ATM and debit card processing expense and smaller decreases and increases in several other expense categories. The efficiency ratio for the current quarter was 53.94% compared to 53.40% for the preceding quarter and 53.18% for the comparable quarter one year ago. For the 2026 fiscal year, operating expenses increased $1.63 million, or 4%, to $47.02 million from $45.39 million for the 2025 fiscal year. The efficiency ratio for the 2026 fiscal year improved to 53.83% from 54.98% for the 2025 fiscal year.

The provision for income taxes for the current quarter increased $32,000, or 2%, to $1.96 million from $1.93 million for the preceding quarter, primarily due to higher taxable income. Timberland’s effective income tax rate was 19.5% for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, compared to 20.0% for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and 18.1% for the quarter ended September 30, 2025. Timberland’s effective income tax rate was 19.9% for fiscal year 2026 compared to 19.5% for fiscal year 2025.

The increase during the quarter was primarily due to an increase in net loans receivable, which was partially offset by decreases in total cash and cash equivalents and investment securities.

Liquidity

An income statement is one of three major financial statements used to evaluate the health of a company, along with the balance sheet and cash flow statement. There are several terms you'll need to understand in order to know how to read an income statement.

An income statement is a financial statement that outlines a company's gains, losses, revenue, and expenses during a specific period.

Also called a Profit and Loss (P&L) Statement or a statement of revenue and expense, the income statement is one of three major documents, along with the cash flow statement and the balance sheet, that provide information on a company's financial results during a specified time frame.

There are several key components of an income statement, and knowing them can go a long way toward helping you interpret one of these documents effectively.

Revenue is the amount of money the company brought in during the reporting period. With revenue, it may be important to note any trends to determine whether the company is making more money over time or if sales are slowing down.

This section, crucial to analyzing an income statement, details how much the company has spent. Similar to revenue, it may be important to note trends to see if the company is spending more or if they're becoming more efficient over time. When looking at expenses, "We should consider whether the expenses grow in proportion to revenue and the drivers of these expenses," says Patrick Badolato, PhD, CPA, an associate professor in the accounting department at the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas.

Expenses can include many different line items, for example interest paid on debt, depreciation and amortization, rent and overhead, as well as money paid toward salaries and benefits.

For the sake of clarity, depreciation is an accounting measure to account for the cost in the loss of value for tangible assets of the company, whereas amortization is an accounting technique to lower the book value of debt over time.

Expenses also include cost of goods sold (COGS), which is the amount spent on the production of the products or services sold. For a company like Apple, it would include the glass to make the phone screen or the chips that go into the iPhone.

Other costs that would be counted under expenses would be operating and non-operating expenses. Operating expenses are the cost to bring the product to the market. This could include things like marketing, payroll, and overhead expenses, such as insurance and rent. Non-operating expenses could include things that do not directly relate to core business functions. It may include things like contributions to pension plans or dividends to shareholders.

Another major consideration is taxes, which of course cuts into any financial results a company generates.

Net income represents the total income left over after all deductions and expenses, including taxes, have been taken out. This is the last line on the income statement, frequently referred to as the bottom line, and it tells you what a company's profit or loss was during a specific time period.

The income statement is important for a wide range of parties, including investors and people responsible for running a company (its executives and managers).

"The income statement should be used by anyone trying to understand the business conducted as well as the profitability of a company," says Badolato.

One simple way an income statement can come in handy is by providing a sense of just how profitable a company really is. Is the company in question making money?

Income statements can help answer this question, along with providing some excellent insight into why, exactly, a company is experiencing its current financial performance.

By reviewing a company's income statement, you can quickly pinpoint areas that have room for improvement. For example, a company could cut costs in one area and put more money into others, such as sales and marketing, that could potentially fuel expansion.

Investors may use income statements, along with other financial statements, to make investing decisions and determine the financial health of a company.

For example, an increasing amount of sales from year to year might be attractive for a potential investor and can be found in the first line of an income statement. Conversely, if costs are rising this can also be seen on the income statement and may lead an investor to ask more questions about the long-term profitability of the company.

Investors and financial analysts also use the income statement to derive popular financial ratios like Earnings Per Share (EPS).

Earnings per share is a measure that compares a company's net income compared to the outstanding shares. The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E ratio, is another commonly used metric that factors in the company's stock price in relation to EPS. When comparing companies, EPS and the P/E ratio can help differentiate two companies in the same category and help an investor make a more sound investing decision, but both use information provided through the income statement.

"The equation driving the Income Statement is: Revenues – Expenses + Gains – Losses = Net Income," says Badolato.

Income statements are also important to regulators. All public companies are required to file a Form 10-K each year with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Form 10-Q each quarter which include the income statement and other financial documents and disclosures.

When analyzing income statements, there are two primary methods that are used: vertical analysis and horizontal analysis.

Vertical analysis shows each item on a financial statement as a percentage. An example of this would be the COGS expressed as 35% of the total revenue. This type of analysis can be useful when comparing with other companies in the industry.

Horizontal analysis is used to review a company's performance over two or more periods by stacking each line item directly next to each other from the previous period. Instead of looking at one income statement at a time from different periods, horizontal analysis compares them side-by-side in one view.

Below is the 2021 quarterly income statement from Ford's Form 10-Q. One of the first things that you will notice is that the report is using horizontal analysis. This is because the report is comparing the second quarter of 2020 to the second quarter of 2021 as well as the first half of 2020 and the first half of 2021.

In the first section under Revenues, you'll see each of Ford's major revenue streams, including car sales under Automotive, Ford Credit, and Mobility. In the notes section of the 10-Q, the Mobility line refers to Ford's autonomous vehicles and related business as well as its equity stake in Argo AI.

Next in the cost and expenses section, you'll notice where Ford is spending its cash. The bulk of those expenses fall under cost of sales, which is another name for the cost of goods sold. You can also see that costs have increased from the second quarter of 2020 to the second quarter of 2021 resulting in a net income of $561 million during the second quarter and $3.8B during the first half of 2021 in the final column on the right.

Both income statements and balance sheets provide important details about how a company uses its cash and other assets, but there are a few key differences between the two.

Think of an income statement like a financial timeline, whereas a balance sheet is a snapshot at one point in time. This is because income statements provide details on the amount of money made and spent during a period. The income statement essentially answers the following questions: How much money did the company make? How was that money spent? Did the company make a profit?

The balance sheet, on the other hand, tells you how much the company has in assets, liabilities and shareholder's equity. The balance sheet follows a simple formula:

Asset = Liabilities + Shareholder's equity

Like the name mentions, the figures on the balance sheet must match as any increases or decreases must be offset. Unlike the income statement, it does not provide information on how much money the company has made or lost, it only provides the amount of debt, cash and other assets that the company owns at that point in time.

While these financial statements are different, both the income statement and balance sheet along with the cash flow statement are still linked and should be used together to determine a more holistic financial picture of a company.

Income statement
Balance sheet

The income statement is a good entry point to understand and evaluate a company's revenue and costs, but it's important to keep in mind that it's not a document that can tell the full story.

"Financial statements are designed to work as a system and not as stand-alone statements," adds Badolato. "The Income Statement is only one piece in understanding the financial performance of a business. Using one financial statement without the others and other publicly available information — such as the footnotes in a financial filing — would be similar to betting before looking at one's cards."

The frequency can vary, but usually, companies prepare income statements either quarterly or annually.

An income statement shows a company's financial performance during a specific time frame, whereas a balance sheet shows a company's assets and liabilities at one point.

Companies release income statements in their financial reports, and you can also find them on the investor relations sections of corporate websites.

An income statement can display a negative net income, which indicates that a company suffered a loss during a specific period.

You can use the information on an income statement to calculate key ratios like gross margin, operating margin and earnings per share.
